tier_reason: bench/ holds coroio and libevent p50 result files for three machines, the run scripts and examples/bench.cpp (25 runs, p50 of sorted microsecond timings); README names CPU and clang 16 for one machine, but no optimization flags or build type are stated anywhere and the bench-libevent program source is not in the repo, so first-party partial methodology: C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 16 on Ubuntu 23.04 for the i7-12800H run (README heading); optimization flags and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE not stated (the root CMakeLists sets no default build type; the library target gets cxx_std_23 and -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror). Benchmark program examples/bench.cpp, built as build/bench; the libevent side is build/bench-libevent, whose source and build are not in the repo. Taskset pinned to CPU 10 with isolcpus/nohz_full and the performance governor per bench/run.sh comments.
corrections.caveats: Author-run on three machines; first-party with partial methodology (flags and build type not stated), so tier C. Mixed result: on the i7-12800H libevent epoll is as fast or faster for 512 to 2048 descriptors (and at 8192 and 32768) with 1 active connection, and coroio is 13-36% slower for 2048 to 32768 descriptors with 100 active connections; the clear wins are at small descriptor counts and on the i5-11400F and M1. On the i5-11400F with 1 active connection coroio is also slightly slower at 1024 and 2048 descriptors (74 vs 70 us, 79 vs 73 us), and the libevent file has no values at 65536 and 131072. The libevent side is libevent's own bench.c built as bench-libevent (build flags and the program source are not in the repo); run_libevent.sh takes the 12th smallest output line while coroio's bench.cpp prints index 12 of 25 sorted runs (13th smallest), a one-rank difference that slightly favors libevent if it prints one line per run. Both sides measure pipe event dispatch, not real socket echo or HTTP serving. No comparison against Boost.Asio or libuv exists in the repo. The actor-ring numbers use baselines outside the listed set and Akka is faster on the local ring. Charts in the README are images; the numbers above were read from bench/*.txt files and compared with a script (ratios derived from page data).

notes: All quoted p50 pairs and ratios re-derived from bench/netlib_* and bench/libevent_* files and match (1.38x at 1, 1.56x at 4, 1.61x 100-active at 1, 1.17-1.74x on 11400F 100-active, 1.47x M1 at 16384). Metadata matches: BSD-2-Clause, 131 stars, last commit 2026-08-06, not a fork.

tier_reason: README Benchmarks section gives CPU (Xeon E5-2620 v4), kernel and clang 10 with the rust_echo_bench table (C++ RECV-SEND 120,239 vs C 114,461 req/s, 105.05%) and demo/bench.cpp is public, but build flags for the measured binaries are not stated and both servers are the author's own: first-party partial methodology, C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang version 10.0.0-4ubuntu1 on Ubuntu 20.04.1, kernel 5.9.0-050900rc6; build flags for the measured binaries not stated (README build instructions use CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and the CMakeLists only adds -fcoroutines for GCC, but neither is tied to the numbers; the load-tool command is cargo run --release).
corrections.caveats: The 105% is an abstraction-parity result against a raw io_uring C server written by the same author, not a win over epoll; 3 runs on one machine (run ranges do not overlap: C RECV-SEND 112,112-116,797 vs C++ 117,519-121,139 req/s) and the numbers appear to date from late 2020 (kernel 5.9.0-rc6 build of 2020-09-23, clang 10); the repo has been restructured since, and where the load generator ran is not stated. The C server (CarterLi/io_uring-echo-server) in its own README reports io_uring POLL-RECV-SEND at 106.70% (-c 50) and 101.79% (-c 200) of its epoll POLL-RECV-SEND server on a 4-vCPU VMware guest (kernel 5.5.0, MacBook Pro i7 2.5GHz host) with clang 9.0.1, so the epoll comparison is indirect, run on different hardware, and within a few percent; in that README the non-poll SEND-RECV mode (the mode of the C++ 105% row) was only 57.34% (-c 50) and 51.40% (-c 200) of epoll on kernel 5.5, so there is no like-for-like epoll figure for the winning row. The other C++ configurations (POLL, SPLICE) are slower than C, and the yield path is about 3% slower than plain NOP. The yield microbench prints std::chrono::high_resolution_clock tick counts for 10,000,000 iterations (nanoseconds on Linux libstdc++/libc++, i.e. about 544 vs 527 ns per operation, derived from page data); units are not printed. First-party with flags not stated, so tier C.
